data.author: Lubna Masarwa

on

Far-right march sparks clashes and leaves several residents injured, as Palestinians fear more attacks
Right-wing Israelis activies argue with left-win protesters outside an Israeli court in the southern Israeli city of Beersheva on 15 June 2022 (AFP)
Off
A far-right Israeli mob marched through Palestinian neighbourhoods in the city of Lod on Sunday night, provoking and assaulting residents and sparking clashes.
Palestinian citizens of Israel said that a group of Jewish Israelis had travelled from outside the city before entering their neighbourhoods late at night.
The group marched through the streets, throwing stones, insulting residents and shouting racist slurs. Clashes broke out as Palestinian residents confronted the mob, leaving several people lightly wounded.
Khaled al-Zabarqa, head of the Popular Committee in Lod, said the incident was the third of its kind over the past month.
It was preceded by a similar provocation near the Al-Omari Mosque, followed by another incident in the central market.
But Sunday's attack involved a group from outside the city, and included an attempt to assault a Palestinian house, he told Middle East Eye.
“This group is trying to ignite tensions in the city for political purposes," he said.
Zabarqa accused police of complicity.
“We had previously alerted the police to these provocations and warned them of the potential consequences. They bear responsibility for what is happening," he said.
“The police knew about yesterday’s incident beforehand. Rather than preventing it, they protected the group and subsequently helped its members evade accountability.
“The failure of the police and state authorities to protect Arab residents points to a systematic policy."

data.author: MEE staff

on

Demonstrators take part in a "Red Line" protest demanding "government action to stop the genocide in Gaza" in Amsterdam on October 5, 2025. (Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP)
Off
Tens of thousands of people marched through Amsterdam on Sunday, demanding that the Dutch government end arms sales to Israel and impose tougher trade sanctions over its genocide in Gaza.
Many wore red for the Red Line protest, which drew more than 200,000 people, according to Amnesty International’s Dutch branch, one of the organisers.
Campaigners called on the Netherlands to formally recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide and denounced Israeli apartheid in the occupied West Bank.
Crowds chanted “Free, free Palestine!”.
“What is happening there is inhumane,” marcher Mike van Dongen told The Associated Press. “As far as I’m concerned, they are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”
Palestinian medical authorities put the death toll in Gaza at 74,643, with 175,962 wounded.
The dead include about 22,000 children, and thousands of people remain missing beneath the rubble.
Since the 11 October 2025 ceasefire, 1,613 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza and 5,833 wounded. Israel’s war on Lebanon has killed more than 4,000 people since March.

"Two days ago I called for the formation of a unity government, and this is the need of the hour," Netanyahu said.
"You cannot form a government with Hamas supporters," he added. "You cannot fight Iran and the rest of its followers within extremist Islam if, inside the government, you rely on supporters of extremist Islam."
Netanyahu said the government should include all parties of the national camp, including Haredi parties, as well as the other Zionist parties, and should be led by Likud.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Anti-Muslim influence campaign targeting UK traced back to Israel
data.author: Imran Mulla
data.summary:
Anti-Muslim influence campaign targeting UK traced back to Israel
Submitted by
Imran Mulla
on
Mon, 11/09/2026 - 14:11
Large numbers of paid advertisements warned of a Qatar-backed Islamic takeover of Britain in run-up to 2024 election and riots
Far-right rioters hurl projectiles at police in Bristol, UK, on 3 August 2024 (Justin Tallis/AFP)
Off
A new investigation has traced a major anti-Muslim propaganda campaign targeting Britain back to Israel.
The campaign, uncovered by academics Marc Owen Jones and Sohan Dsouza, was at its height before the UK's 2024 general election and the anti-Muslim riots that raged across the country later that year.
It involved large numbers of paid advertisements warning of an Islamic takeover of Britain masterminded by Qatar.
"Between 2024 and 2026, our investigation recorded more than 154m exposures to its British-targeted material," Jones and Dsouza wrote in an article published by The Nerve.
"Its first wave of British advertising ran in the months before the 2024 general election. The ads were also hammering the UK in the winter and spring leading up to the anti-Muslim riots that followed the Southport murders."
In July 2024, violent disorder raged in cities and towns across Britain, targeting Muslims and ethnic minorities, after the murder of three young girls in Southport by Axel Rudakubana.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Senior UAE official says Gulf faces 'prolonged uncertainty' with no settlement to Iran war
data.author: Hossam Desouky
data.summary:
Senior UAE official says Gulf faces 'prolonged uncertainty' with no settlement to Iran war
A senior UAE official warned that the Gulf must be prepared for a “long period of uncertainty” in which the US and Iran are not able to come to a political settlement to end their war, leaving the region in a state of limbo.
"We should... prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, said on Monday at a forum in Abu Dhabi.
Gargash’s remarks come as the Middle East tries to decipher whether US President Donald Trump will launch fresh strikes on Iran.
Expectations of a new attack were high until last week, when on 3 November the Democrats won a sweeping midterm election victory that Trump and Vice President JD Vance attributed to the unpopularity of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Trump told CNN on Monday it was “highly unlikely” he would attack while negotiations are ongoing.
